solution:
Treat each oxygen molecule as a sphere of diameter \(d = 3\,\mathring{A}\), so radius \(r = 1.5 \times 10^{-10}\,\text{m}\).

Volume of one molecule \(= \tfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3 = \tfrac{4}{3}\pi (1.5 \times 10^{-10})^3 = 1.41 \times 10^{-29}\,\text{m}^3\).

One mole contains \(N_A = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\) molecules, so the molecular volume of one mole is

\(V_{\text{mol}} = 6.022 \times 10^{23} \times 1.41 \times 10^{-29} = 8.51 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{m}^3\)

At STP one mole of an ideal gas actually occupies \(V = 22.4\,\text{litre} = 22.4 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{m}^3\).

Hence the required fraction is

\(\dfrac{V_{\text{mol}}}{V} = \dfrac{8.51 \times 10^{-6}}{22.4 \times 10^{-3}} = 3.8 \times 10^{-4}\)

The molecules themselves occupy only about \(3.8 \times 10^{-4}\) of the volume of the gas, i.e. roughly \(0.04\,\%\) — which is why the free-molecule (ideal gas) picture works so well.

For one mole of an ideal gas, \(PV = \mu RT\) with \(\mu = 1\), so

\(V = \dfrac{RT}{P}\)

At STP the pressure is one atmosphere, \(P = 1.013 \times 10^{5}\,\text{Pa}\), and the temperature is \(0^\circ\text{C} = 273\,\text{K}\). With \(R = 8.31\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}\),

\(V = \dfrac{8.31 \times 273}{1.013 \times 10^{5}} = \dfrac{2268.6}{1.013 \times 10^{5}} = 2.24 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{m}^3\)

Since \(1\,\text{m}^3 = 10^3\,\text{litre}\),

\(V = 22.4 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{m}^3 = 22.4\,\text{litre}\)

Note that \(V\) depends only on \(P\) and \(T\) and not on the identity of the gas, so \(22.4\) litre per mole at STP is the same for every ideal gas.

The dotted plot is a horizontal straight line: \(PV/T\) has the same value at every pressure.

For \(\mu\) moles of an ideal gas \(PV = \mu RT\), so \(PV/T = \mu R\), a constant independent of \(P\) and \(T\). A horizontal line is therefore exactly what an ideal gas would give.

Here \(\mu = \dfrac{1.00 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{kg}}{32.0 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{kg mol}^{-1}} = 3.125 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{mol}\), so the dotted line sits at

\(\dfrac{PV}{T} = \mu R = 3.125 \times 10^{-2} \times 8.31 = 0.26\,\text{J K}^{-1}\)

The dotted plot signifies ideal-gas behaviour: \(PV/T\) constant at \(\mu R = 0.26\,\text{J K}^{-1}\) for this \(1\,\text{g}\) sample of oxygen, whatever the pressure.

A real gas approaches ideal behaviour at low pressure and HIGH temperature, so of two curves the one lying closer to the horizontal ideal-gas line over the plotted range is the one at the higher temperature.

In Fig. 12.8 the curve labelled \(T_1\) stays nearer the dotted line, while the \(T_2\) curve dips further below it before rising — a larger departure from ideal behaviour.

Hence \(T_1 > T_2\).

The curves meet the \(y\)-axis in the limit \(P \rightarrow 0\). At vanishing pressure the molecules are far apart, intermolecular forces are negligible and every real gas becomes ideal, so both curves must converge on the ideal value \(PV/T = \mu R\).

Number of moles of oxygen:

\(\mu = \dfrac{m}{M_0} = \dfrac{1.00 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{kg}}{32.0 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{kg mol}^{-1}} = 3.125 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{mol}\)

Therefore

\(\dfrac{PV}{T} = \mu R = 3.125 \times 10^{-2} \times 8.31 = 0.26\,\text{J K}^{-1}\)

The curves meet the \(y\)-axis at \(PV/T = 0.26\,\text{J K}^{-1}\).

No. The intercept is \(PV/T = \mu R = (m/M_0)R\), which depends on the MOLAR MASS as well as the mass. For the same \(m = 1.00 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{kg}\) of hydrogen,

\(\mu_{\text{H}_2} = \dfrac{1.00 \times 10^{-3}}{2.02 \times 10^{-3}} = 0.495\,\text{mol}\), giving \(PV/T = 0.495 \times 8.31 = 4.11\,\text{J K}^{-1}\)

which is about 16 times the oxygen value of \(0.26\,\text{J K}^{-1}\). So the intercept is NOT the same.

To obtain the same intercept the two gases must contain the same number of moles, \(\mu = 3.125 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{mol}\). The required mass of hydrogen is

\(m_{\text{H}_2} = \mu M_0 = 3.125 \times 10^{-2} \times 2.02\,\text{g} = 6.3 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{g}\)

Equivalently \(m_{\text{H}_2} = m_{\text{O}_2} \times \dfrac{2.02}{32.0} = 1.00\,\text{g} \times 0.0631\).

Required mass of hydrogen \(= 6.3 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{g} = 6.3 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{kg}\).

The pressures quoted are GAUGE pressures, so the absolute pressures are one atmosphere higher:

\(P_1 = 15 + 1 = 16\,\text{atm} = 16 \times 1.013 \times 10^{5} = 1.621 \times 10^{6}\,\text{Pa}\), \(T_1 = 27^\circ\text{C} = 300\,\text{K}\)

\(P_2 = 11 + 1 = 12\,\text{atm} = 12 \times 1.013 \times 10^{5} = 1.216 \times 10^{6}\,\text{Pa}\), \(T_2 = 17^\circ\text{C} = 290\,\text{K}\)

The volume is fixed at \(V = 30\,\text{litre} = 30 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{m}^3\). From \(PV = \mu RT\),

\(\mu_1 = \dfrac{P_1 V}{R T_1} = \dfrac{1.621 \times 10^{6} \times 30 \times 10^{-3}}{8.31 \times 300} = 19.50\,\text{mol}\)

\(\mu_2 = \dfrac{P_2 V}{R T_2} = \dfrac{1.216 \times 10^{6} \times 30 \times 10^{-3}}{8.31 \times 290} = 15.13\,\text{mol}\)

Moles withdrawn \(= 19.50 - 15.13 = 4.37\,\text{mol}\). With molar mass \(M_0 = 32\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\),

\(\Delta m = 4.37 \times 32 = 139.9\,\text{g}\)

Mass of oxygen taken out \(\approx 0.14\,\text{kg}\).

(Reading the 15 atm and 11 atm as absolute pressures instead gives \(18.29 - 13.87 = 4.42\,\text{mol}\) and \(141\,\text{g}\) — the same \(0.14\,\text{kg}\) to two significant figures, so the answer does not turn on the gauge/absolute distinction.)

The amount of gas in the bubble is unchanged, so \(\dfrac{P_1 V_1}{T_1} = \dfrac{P_2 V_2}{T_2}\).

At the bottom the pressure is atmospheric plus the water column:

\(P_1 = P_0 + \rho g h = 1.01 \times 10^{5} + 1000 \times 9.8 \times 40 = 1.01 \times 10^{5} + 3.92 \times 10^{5} = 4.93 \times 10^{5}\,\text{Pa}\)

At the surface \(P_2 = P_0 = 1.01 \times 10^{5}\,\text{Pa}\).

Temperatures: \(T_1 = 12^\circ\text{C} = 285\,\text{K}\), \(T_2 = 35^\circ\text{C} = 308\,\text{K}\); and \(V_1 = 1.0\,\text{cm}^3\).

\(V_2 = V_1 \times \dfrac{P_1}{P_2} \times \dfrac{T_2}{T_1} = 1.0 \times \dfrac{4.93 \times 10^{5}}{1.01 \times 10^{5}} \times \dfrac{308}{285}\)

\(V_2 = 1.0 \times 4.88 \times 1.081 = 5.3\,\text{cm}^3\)

The bubble grows to \(V_2 \approx 5.3\,\text{cm}^3 = 5.3 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{m}^3\).

Avogadro's hypothesis makes the number of molecules independent of which gases are present, so the mixed composition of air does not matter. Using \(PV = k_B N T\),

\(N = \dfrac{PV}{k_B T}\)

with \(P = 1\,\text{atm} = 1.01 \times 10^{5}\,\text{Pa}\), \(V = 25.0\,\text{m}^3\), \(T = 27^\circ\text{C} = 300\,\text{K}\) and \(k_B = 1.38 \times 10^{-23}\,\text{J K}^{-1}\):

\(N = \dfrac{1.01 \times 10^{5} \times 25.0}{1.38 \times 10^{-23} \times 300} = \dfrac{2.525 \times 10^{6}}{4.14 \times 10^{-21}}\)

\(N = 6.1 \times 10^{26}\) molecules.

Helium is monatomic, so a helium atom has only the three translational degrees of freedom and its average thermal energy is

\(E = \dfrac{3}{2} k_B T\), with \(k_B = 1.38 \times 10^{-23}\,\text{J K}^{-1}\)

(i) \(T = 27^\circ\text{C} = 300\,\text{K}\):

\(E = 1.5 \times 1.38 \times 10^{-23} \times 300 = 6.21 \times 10^{-21}\,\text{J}\)

(ii) \(T = 6000\,\text{K}\):

\(E = 1.5 \times 1.38 \times 10^{-23} \times 6000 = 1.24 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J}\)

(iii) \(T = 10^{7}\,\text{K}\):

\(E = 1.5 \times 1.38 \times 10^{-23} \times 10^{7} = 2.07 \times 10^{-16}\,\text{J}\)

(i) \(6.21 \times 10^{-21}\,\text{J}\); (ii) \(1.24 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J}\); (iii) \(2.07 \times 10^{-16}\,\text{J}\).

Number of molecules: from \(PV = k_B N T\), \(N = PV/(k_B T)\). Since \(P\), \(V\) and \(T\) are the same for all three vessels, \(N\) is the same — this is Avogadro's hypothesis, and it does not care whether the gas is monatomic, diatomic or polyatomic. So YES, the three vessels contain equal numbers of molecules.

Root mean square speed: \(\tfrac{1}{2} m v_{\text{rms}}^2 = \tfrac{3}{2} k_B T\), so

\(v_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{3 k_B T}{m}}\)

At a common temperature \(v_{\text{rms}} \propto 1/\sqrt{m}\), so it is NOT the same in the three cases — it is largest for the lightest molecule.

The molecular masses are neon \(20.2\,\text{u}\), chlorine \((\text{Cl}_2)\) \(70.9\,\text{u}\) and uranium hexafluoride \((\text{UF}_6)\) \(238 + 6 \times 19 = 352\,\text{u}\). Neon is by far the lightest.

Yes, all three contain equal numbers of molecules; no, \(v_{\text{rms}}\) is not the same, and it is largest for NEON.

For a gas of molar mass \(M_0\), \(v_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{3RT/M_0}\). Setting the argon and helium speeds equal,

\(\dfrac{3 R T_{\text{Ar}}}{M_{\text{Ar}}} = \dfrac{3 R T_{\text{He}}}{M_{\text{He}}}\)

so

\(T_{\text{Ar}} = T_{\text{He}} \times \dfrac{M_{\text{Ar}}}{M_{\text{He}}}\)

With \(T_{\text{He}} = -20^\circ\text{C} = 253\,\text{K}\), \(M_{\text{Ar}} = 39.9\,\text{u}\) and \(M_{\text{He}} = 4.0\,\text{u}\):

\(T_{\text{Ar}} = 253 \times \dfrac{39.9}{4.0} = 253 \times 9.975 = 2.52 \times 10^{3}\,\text{K}\)

The argon must be at \(T \approx 2.52 \times 10^{3}\,\text{K}\) (about \(2.25 \times 10^{3}\,^\circ\text{C}\)). Note the answer is a temperature ratio, so it does not depend on \(R\).

[Textbook answer-key error: the printed key gives the mean free path as \(1.0 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{m}\), but that value is not reachable from the key's OWN numbers. Substituting the key's own printed number density \(n = 5.10 \times 10^{25}\,\text{m}^{-3}\) into the standard \(l = 1/(\sqrt{2}\,\pi n d^{2})\) with \(d = 2\,\text{Å}\) gives \(1.10 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{m}\), which does not round to \(1.0\) at two significant figures. The value below is derived independently and agrees with that. The mechanism behind the printed figure is UNCONFIRMED — dropping the \(\sqrt{2}\), dropping the \(\pi\), using \(\sqrt{2\pi}\), or taking a different molecular diameter each give something else — so no single slip is asserted. Note the key's collision frequency \(\nu \approx 5.1 \times 10^{9}\,\text{s}^{-1}\) is consistent WITH its low \(l\) rather than being a second error: it simply inherits it. Everything else in that key entry agrees.] The molecular diameter is \(d = 2r = 2.0 \times 10^{-10}\,\text{m}\), and \(T = 17^\circ\text{C} = 290\,\text{K}\), \(P = 2.0\,\text{atm} = 2.026 \times 10^{5}\,\text{Pa}\).

Number density:

\(n = \dfrac{P}{k_B T} = \dfrac{2.026 \times 10^{5}}{1.38 \times 10^{-23} \times 290} = 5.06 \times 10^{25}\,\text{m}^{-3}\)

Mean free path, from \(l = 1/(\sqrt{2}\,n \pi d^2)\):

\(l = \dfrac{1}{1.414 \times 5.06 \times 10^{25} \times \pi \times (2.0 \times 10^{-10})^2} = 1.11 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{m}\)

The rms speed of a nitrogen molecule \((M_0 = 28.0 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{kg mol}^{-1})\) is

\(v_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{3RT}{M_0}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{3 \times 8.31 \times 290}{28.0 \times 10^{-3}}} = 508\,\text{m s}^{-1}\)

Collision frequency:

\(\nu = \dfrac{v_{\text{rms}}}{l} = \dfrac{508}{1.11 \times 10^{-7}} = 4.6 \times 10^{9}\,\text{s}^{-1}\)

For the comparison, the collision itself lasts about the time needed to cross one molecular diameter, while the free flight lasts the time needed to cross one mean free path:

\(t_{\text{collision}} = \dfrac{d}{v_{\text{rms}}} = \dfrac{2.0 \times 10^{-10}}{508} = 3.9 \times 10^{-13}\,\text{s}\)

\(t_{\text{free}} = \dfrac{l}{v_{\text{rms}}} = \dfrac{1.11 \times 10^{-7}}{508} = 2.2 \times 10^{-10}\,\text{s}\)

\(\dfrac{t_{\text{free}}}{t_{\text{collision}}} = \dfrac{l}{d} = \dfrac{1.11 \times 10^{-7}}{2.0 \times 10^{-10}} \approx 5.6 \times 10^{2}\)

Mean free path \(l = 1.11 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{m}\); collision frequency \(\nu = 4.6 \times 10^{9}\,\text{s}^{-1}\); and the molecule spends about \(500\) times longer in free flight than in collision.
